newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban in dilemma - fight or talk?.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban in dilemma - fight or talk?.

text.p: Two weeks after their dramatic capture of Kabul, Afghan's Taleban militia faced a major dilemma on Friday on whether to talk or fight after their most powerful opponents forged a new military alliance.

The Taleban said it was ready for talks with its foes, and a spokesman warned that northern Uzbek militia chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum and former government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood would be responsible for "bad results" if they rejected negotiations.
"We call on both of them for talks," said Maulvi Wakil Ahmad, a member of the Taleban supreme shura (council), contacted in the Pakistani border city of Quetta.
"They must not select the path of fighting because this is a bloody path," he said. "If they impose fighting on the government, the government will strongly defend itself."

On Thursday, United Nations Special envoy Norbert Holl flew to Kabul to call for a ceasefire after Masood, in ferocious battles, inflicted the worst reverses on the Taleban in their two years of existence.

Dostum, Masood and Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat leader Karim Khalili signed a pact in northern Afghanistan on Thursday to jointly fight the Taleban, born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, if any of them came under attack.
"Whoever is not ceasing to fight against one of the signatories, the other signatories will jointly fight against them," Dostum spokesman Mohammed Yusuf told reporters.

The Taleban, who seized the Afghan capital on September 27, have previously said they have no quarrel with Dostum, who controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces, but insist that all Afghan factions must be disarmed.

The anti-Taleban alliance, composed of groups that have fought each other bitterly in the past, could pose a serious challenge to the Islamic militants, who have already suffered battlefield reverses to Masood's forces this week.

The alliance also called for a meeting of all faction leaders in Mazar-i-Sharif, Dostum's headquarters, to form "a permanent government of Afghanistan" and agreed to set up a Supreme Defence Council whose composition was to be decided later.

Afghan watchers in Kabul said there were hopes that the Taleban would accept the invitation to talks implicit in the call for a meeting of all factions, if the pragmatists in the movement had the upper hand.
One noted that acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous had called for a similar meeting.
Ghous has also said Masood would be forgiven if he surrendered and would be allowed to take part in a government to be decided on by a national convention.

"I don't think these positions are very far apart, but Ghous may not be speaking for all of the Taleban movement," said one veteran Afghan watcher. "There are some real hardliners for whom finishing the Jihad (Holy War) and a nationwide imposition of (Islamic) Sharia law is the only thing."
The Taleban say they are dedicated to completing the war for an Islamic state begun in 1979 when the Soviet army moved in to back a communist government in Kabul.
For both purist and pragmatic Taleban, Dostum is a major problem. A former communist who switched sides in 1992, he runs a liberal Islamic regime which the purists abhor.
He also has probably the best equipped fighting force in Afghanistan and his Uzbeks, descendants of the Mongols of Genghis Khan, are feared as tough fighters.

He has a small air force and at his back are the nations of Central Asia who, along with Russia, have expressed fears publicly of any push by the Taleban and their harsh Islamic Sharia law across their borders.
Dostum had already moved armour and men south of the Salang Tunnel that links Kabul with northern Afghanistan.
Morale among the black-turbanned Taleban appears to be an increasing problem.
They had few serious setbacks as they swept to power in three-quarters of Afghanistan and pushed north to bottle up Masood in his Panjsher valley fortress after they took Kabul.

But four days of fighting gave them only a toe-hold in the gorge leading into the Panjsher before Masood launched a stunning counter-attack in the Salang Pass which leads through the Hindu Kush to Dostum territory.

Journalists have been barred from the front since it became apparent that the Taleban were taking heavy casualties, but witnesses say they have seen scores of dead and wounded being ferried south since the battle began on Tuesday.
Taleban fighters manning roadblocks on the road north from Kabul have lost their cheery readiness to discuss the fighting and turned surly and sometimes aggressive.

Travellers said the Taleban had massed 2,000 men at Charikar, a half-hour drive south of the front-line town of Jabal-os-Saraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass in another sign that the tide may have turned against them.
